source_document.body:
EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
FedEx Driver Finds Plymouth Road Runner Rotting in Yard, It Was the 1970 Hemi 4-Speed Pilot Car
75 photos
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews
“These are my keeper cars and ones that I just uh have a lot of meaning for me and I'm going to keep for as long as I can.” To say that Dale Mathews is a car collector is like saying rain is wet. The Lenoir, North Carolina Moparhead is a larger-than-life car addict (do you have a better word?), and his collection includes some really impressive machines with equally amazing stories.
While most Mopar collectors lose sleep chasing numbers-matching hardware, Dale owns an Alpine White 1970 Plymouth Road Runner whose factory parts break every rule in the restoration manual. Featured on the Cars Over Coffee episode from the Cherries Media YouTube channel, chassis RM21R0A100015 is not a botched backyard mashup.
It is the documented one-of-one 1970 Hemi Road Runner Pilot Car—the very first 1970 Road Runner coupe Plymouth ever assembled.
Its resurrection began in 1999 when Mathews' friend, FedEx driver Ken Lewis, spotted a battered blue shell languishing in a local yard and dialed Mathews with news of a real 1970 Hemi car. Following a divorce, the previous owner had hauled off the rusty, windshield-less body while leaving scattered components behind in his former basement, and its original engine had vanished decades earlier.
Photo: YouTube/Road Test TV Crucially, the dash VIN tag, body numbers, and badly rust-cancer corroded fender tag reading PILOT survived intact. The seller already knew he possessed a rare bird—having secured a 1991 verification letter from Mopar registrar Galen Govier—and initially refused to part with it. Not the one to back down or take “No” for a definitive answer, Mathews visited repeatedly before planting a firm $6,000 offer in the man's mind at a time when local buyers might have floated $1,500, and called it “generous.”
When cash grew tight, the phone rang, and Mathews immediately trailered his rusted prize down to an Atlanta Mopar show so Govier could inspect it firsthand. Decoding RM21R0A100015 reveals a fascinating pre-production timeline straight from Detroit's Lynch Road plant. Its fender tag carries Sales Bank order number M04101 and a scheduled production date of August 1, 1969.
While that was the official opening day of 1970 model-year assembly, multiple March 1969 date codes stamped into the original glass and seat belts prove engineers hand-built it around April 1969. Even more astonishing, Govier concluded with 99% certainty that Mathews' car is the exact coupe photographed for Chrysler's September 1969 press release.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews Teardown and restoration by Hodge Restorations of Inman, South Carolina exposed a forensic wonderland proving this hand-crafted mule bridged two model years. Built atop a 1969 B-body unibody wrapped in 1970 exterior sheetmetal, the chassis was never factory-dipped; workers hand-painted Alpine White across the entire undercarriage, cowl, package tray, and roof.
Its hood emblem opening was cut round, its hood lacked front-trim holes, and it carried a Dodge Charger or Coronet radiator support—complete with three latch-tray studs—stamped with its Plymouth VIN.
Every corner revealed experimental fingerprints that regular assembly-line workers never saw. The firewall retained the 1969 Air Grabber cable hole location instead of 1970 vacuum-hose routing, while 1969 inner fenders featured mounting provisions for both 1969 and 1970 battery trays. Opening the trunk exposes unique prototype reinforcement braces stamped with part number 000 that never reached production, alongside added taillight-panel brackets.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews Inside, its untouched 1969 sweep-style speedometer dash and glovebox badge make it the sole known 1970 Road Runner lacking round Rallye gauges. Optioned like a pure street-strip assassin, the Alpine White post coupe wears black vinyl bench-seat trim, code M2X9, body-colored steel wheels with dog-dish hubcaps, and Goodyear Polyglas GT tires.
Under the functional Air Grabber hood thunders a dual-quad 426 Street Hemi rated at 425 horsepower and 490 lb-ft of torque, feeding an A-833 4-speed and Dana 60 axle via what may be the first Hurst Pistol Grip shifter ever fitted. Former detective and MCACN head judge Frank Badalson personally authenticated every clue ahead of its 2024 MCACN unveiling.
That no-frills, maximum-velocity ethos captured the exact spirit that birthed the Road Runner moniker just two model years earlier. By 1967, American muscle cars like Pontiac's GTO and Plymouth's own plush GTX had bloated in weight and price, pricing out young blue-collar buyers. Product planner Jack Smith and designer Gordon Cherry pitched a stripped-down, sub-$3,000 Belvedere street brawler built for 14-second quarter-miles.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews Chrysler paid Warner Bros. $50,000 for the cartoon bird's rights and spent $10,000 crafting its iconic Beep Beep horn. Debuting for 1968 with a heavy-duty suspension and a standard 335-horsepower 383 V8 borrowing big-valve heads and camshaft hardware from the 440, the Road Runner detonated showroom projections. Plymouth hoped to sell 20,000 cars yet moved 44,313 units in its rookie season, including 1,009 Hemi-powered beasts.
Adding a convertible, optional Air Grabber hood, and the ferocious mid-year 440 Six-Barrel pushed 1969 volume to an all-time record of 84,420 worldwide deliveries—81,125 domestic—and earned Motor Trend's prestigious Car of the Year crown.
Refreshed front and rear sheetmetal, high-back seats, wild High-Impact hues, and the Pistol Grip shifter made 1970 the visual peak of first-generation Road Runner aggression. Nevertheless, punishing muscle-car insurance surcharges and friendly fire from Plymouth's bargain-priced compact Duster 340 slashed production nearly in half to 41,484 worldwide units, representing 36,861 American deliveries, excluding the 1,935 NASCAR-homologated Superbirds.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews 1970 also marked the final curtain for both the rigid pillared coupe body style and the open-air convertible.
Even amid inflation, Plymouth fought hard to defend its budget-muscle roots on 1970 window stickers. The stripped RM21 two-door pillared coupe—the exact configuration of Mathews' Pilot Car—started at just $2,896, while the pillarless RM23 hardtop opened at $3,034 and the RM27 convertible listed at $3,289.
Stepping up from the standard 335-horsepower 383 Road Runner V8 to the 390-horsepower 440 Six-Barrel added $250, whereas ordering the legendary 426 Street Hemi demanded an eye-watering $841 before mandatory Track Pak drivetrain and suspension upgrades.
Photo: YouTube/Cherries Media Among domestic market deliveries, 34,894 Road Runners carried the standard-issue 383—including 14,057 coupes with 5,839 manual 4-speeds—while 1,815 packed the 440 Six-Barrel (1,130 hardtops, 651 coupes, and 34 convertibles). Just 152 received the 426 Hemi: 75 hardtops (59 manuals and 16 automatics), 74 coupes (44 manuals and 30 automatics), and three convertibles, one manual and two autos.
Following that 1970 climax, emissions choke-holds and fuel crises steadily eroded the Road Runner's ferocious bite over its remaining decade. Second-generation fuselage B-bodies slumped to 13,664 units in 1971—the Hemi's swansong with just 55 built—7,628 in 1972, a brief rebound to 19,056 in 1973, and 11,355 in 1974.
After 7,183 Fury-based hardtops closed its standalone B-body run in 1975, the badge shrank into a compact Volaré trim package from 1976 through 1980, sliding from 8,769 in 1976 and 6,975 in 1977 to 1,357 in 1978 and just 496 final 318-powered cars in 1980.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews Standing at the very headwaters of 1970 production as the first of 44 Hemi 4-speed coupes—and the lone factory prototype linking 1969 and 1970—RM21R0A100015 belongs in a museum wing. Yet Mathews rejects static velvet-rope ownership, regularly rowing that historic Pistol Grip shifter across North Carolina backroads just to feel the synchros engage.
Saved from a rusty yard for a stratospheric $6,000, Plymouth's primal 1970 Road Runner still runs fast, loud, and fiercely alive exactly as Detroit built it to run.
